title: Physical distribution

match.reason: No point in the bank covers physical distribution; the closest ones, such as choosing a location and resources needed to start, deal with setting up a business rather than moving goods to customers.

draft.title: Physical distribution
card: Physical distribution is the movement of goods from the producer to the place where customers buy them. It has three main parts: transport, warehousing and stock control.
moves goods by road, rail, sea or air. A business weighs cost, speed and the risk of damage, and the best mode depends on the product.
stores goods until they are needed. Holding stock close to customers can shorten delivery times.
keeps track of how much stock a business holds. Too little stock can mean lost sales, and too much ties up money and storage space.
draft.remember: Physical distribution gets the right goods to the right place at the right time, at a sensible cost.

a.q: Which activity is part of physical distribution?
opts: Storing goods in a warehouse until stores order them
Setting a markup on the cost of making a product
Running television advertisements for a new product
Choosing a retailer to carry a brand's products
a.why: Storing goods until they are needed is warehousing, which is one part of physical distribution. Choosing a retailer is a decision about the distribution channel, not about moving and storing the goods.
a.clue: Look for the option about moving or holding goods.

b.q: Jess sells garden tools online from Orange. Customers complain that popular items are often out of stock for weeks, while slow sellers fill her shed. Which part of physical distribution needs most attention?
opts: Stock control, to match stock held to customer demand
Transport, to deliver parcels by air instead of road
Warehousing, to rent a much larger storage building
Transport, to lower the price of each delivery
b.why: The problem is holding the wrong amounts of each item, which is a stock control issue. A larger shed or faster delivery would not fix the mix of stock, so warehousing and transport are the tempting but wrong choices.
b.clue: The problem is which items she holds, not how they move.

a.best: Storing goods in a warehouse until stores order them

b.best: Stock control, to match stock held to customer demand
